content.paragraph: So far we have considered special types of surfaces: cylinders, quadric surfaces, graphs of functions of two variables, and level surfaces of functions of three variables. Here we use vector functions to describe more general surfaces, called parametric surfaces, and compute their areas. Then we take the general surface area formula and see how it applies to special surfaces.

subsection.title: Parametric Surfaces

subsection.paragraph: In much the same way that we describe a space curve by a vector function $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ of a single parameter $$t$$ , we can describe a surface by a vector function $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ of two parameters $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ . We suppose that

is a vector-valued function defined on a region $$D$$ in the $$u\upsilon$$-plane. So $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ , the component functions of $$\mathbf{r}$$ , are functions of the two variables $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ with domain $$D$$ . The set of all points $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ in $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ such that

and $$\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ varies throughout $$D$$ , is called a parametric surface $$S$$ and Equations 2 are called parametric equations of $$S$$ . Each choice of $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ gives a point on $$S$$ ; by making all choices, we get all of $$S$$ . In other words, the surface $$S$$ is traced out by the tip of the position vector $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ as $$\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ moves throughout the region $$D$$ . (See Figure 1.)

subsection.paragraph: If a parametric surface $$S$$ is given by a vector function $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ , then there are two useful families of curves that lie on $$S$$ , one family with $$u$$ constant and the other with $$\upsilon$$ constant. These families correspond to vertical and horizontal lines in the $$u\upsilon$$-plane. If we keep $$u$$ constant by putting $$u = u_{0}$$ , then $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon} \right)$$ becomes a vector function of the single parameter $$\upsilon$$ and defines a curve $$C_{1}$$ lying on $$S$$ . (See Figure 4.)

subsection.paragraph: Similarly, if we keep $$\upsilon$$ constant by putting $$\upsilon = \upsilon_{0}$$ , we get a curve $$C_{2}$$ given by $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon_{0}} \right)$$ that lies on $$S$$ . We call these curves grid curves. (In Example 1, for instance, the grid curves obtained by letting $$u$$ be constant are horizontal lines, whereas the grid curves with $$\upsilon$$ constant are circles.) In fact, when a computer graphs a parametric surface, it sometimes depicts the surface by plotting these grid curves, as we will see in the following example.

problem.paragraph: Use a computer to graph the surface
Which grid curves have $$u$$ constant? Which have $$\upsilon$$ constant?

Solution We graph the portion of the surface with parameter domain $$0 \leqslant u \leqslant 4\pi$$ , $$0 \leqslant \upsilon \leqslant 2\pi$$ in Figure 5. It has the appearance of a spiral tube. To identify the grid curves, we write the corresponding parametric equations:

If $$\upsilon$$ is constant, then $$\sin\upsilon$$ and $$\cos\upsilon$$ are constant, so the parametric equations resemble those of the helix in Example 13.1.4. Thus the grid curves with $$\upsilon$$ constant are the spiral curves in Figure 5. We deduce that the grid curves with $$u$$ constant must be the curves that look like circles in the figure. Further evidence for this assertion is that if $$u$$ is kept constant, $$u = u_{0}$$ , then the equation $$z = u_{0} + \cos\upsilon$$ shows that the $$z$$-values vary from $$u_{0} - 1$$ to $$u_{0} + 1$$ .

subsection.paragraph: In Examples 1 and 2 we were given a vector equation and asked to graph the corresponding parametric surface. In the following examples, however, we are given the more challenging problem of finding a vector function to represent a given surface. In the rest of this chapter we will often need to do exactly that.

(Figure 6 illustrates how this works, by means of the Parallelogram Law, for the case where $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ are positive. See also Exercise 12.2.46.) Solution The sphere has a simple representation $$\rho = a$$ in spherical coordinates, so let’s choose the angles $$\phi$$ and $$\theta$$ in spherical coordinates as the parameters (see Section 15.8). Then, putting $$\rho = a$$ in the equations for conversion from spherical to rectangular coordinates (Equations 15.8.1), we obtain

We have $$0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi$$ and $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , so the parameter domain is the rectangle $$D = \left\lbrack {0,\pi} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,2\pi} \right\rbrack$$ . The grid curves with $$\phi$$ constant are the circles of constant latitude (including the equator). subsection.paragraph: Note We saw in Example 4 that the grid curves for a sphere are curves of constant latitude or constant longitude. For a general parametric surface we are really making a map and the grid curves are similar to lines of latitude and longitude. Describing a point on a parametric surface (like the one in Figure 5) by giving specific values of $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ is like giving the latitude and longitude of a point.

subsection.paragraph: We now find the tangent plane to a parametric surface $$S$$ traced out by a vector function

at a point $$P_{0}$$ with position vector $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)$$ . If we keep $$u$$ constant by putting $$u = u_{0}$$ , then $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon} \right)$$ becomes a vector function of the single parameter $$\upsilon$$ and defines a grid curve $$C_{1}$$ lying on $$S$$ . (See Figure 14.) The tangent vector to $$C_{1}$$ at $$P_{0}$$ is obtained by taking the partial derivative of $$\mathbf{r}$$ with respect to $$\upsilon$$ :

Similarly, if we keep $$\upsilon$$ constant by putting $$\upsilon = \upsilon_{0}$$ , we get a grid curve $$C_{2}$$ given by $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon_{0}} \right)$$ that lies on $$S$$ , and its tangent vector at $$P_{0}$$ is

If $$\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}$$ is not $$0$$ , then the surface $$S$$ is called smooth (it has no “corners”). For a smooth surface, the tangent plane is the plane that contains the tangent vectors $$\mathbf{r}_{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}$$ , and the vector $$\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}$$ is a normal vector to the tangent plane.
